u.src: Arrayed in two ranks below them were some hundred leaders, great and small, every one fully armed and accoutred, their armor immaculate, their bearing awe-inspiring, and a murderous air rising about them.

p.src: At the sight, the Pilgrim rejoiced inwardly and felt not the least fear. He strode straight through the gate, removed his clapper and bell, and called toward the dais, “Great Kings!” The three old demons asked with genial smiles, “Little Wind-Cleaver, you are back?” The Pilgrim answered, “I am.” “You went to patrol the mountain. What did you learn of Sun the Pilgrim’s whereabouts?” The Pilgrim said, “With Your Majesties above me, I hardly dare speak of it.” The old demon said, “Why do you not dare?” The Pilgrim said, “At Your Majesties’ command, I was walking along sounding my clapper and bell when I suddenly looked up and saw a man crouching there, sharpening a cudgel. He looked like a colossal road-opening deity, and if he stood upright, he must have been well over a hundred feet tall. There on a rock beside the ravine he scooped up a handful of water and sharpened it again. As he worked, he muttered that his cudgel had yet to display its divine power since arriving here; once he had polished it bright, he would come and strike Your Majesties. That was how I knew he was Sun the Pilgrim, and I came especially to report it.”

p.src: When the old demon heard this, sweat broke out all over him. Trembling with fright, he said, “Brothers, I told you not to provoke Tang Sanzang. His disciple possesses tremendous divine powers. He has prepared in advance and is sharpening his cudgel to beat us. What are we to do?” He ordered, “Minions, call in everyone from outside the cave, great and small. Shut the gates and let him pass us by.” One of the leaders who knew the situation reported, “Great King, all the lesser demons outside the gates have already scattered.” The old demon said, “Why have they all scattered? They must have heard that trouble was coming. Quickly, shut the gates! Quickly, shut the gates!” With a great clatter, the demons bolted and barred every gate, front and rear.

p.src: The Pilgrim was inwardly alarmed. “Now that they have shut the gates, if they ask me about my family and background and I cannot answer, will I not give myself away and be seized? I had better frighten them once more and make them leave the gates open, so I can escape.” He stepped forward again and said, “Great Kings, he also said something dreadful.” The old demon asked, “What else did he say?” The Pilgrim said, “He said he would skin the First Great King, scrape the flesh from the Second Great King’s bones, and pull out the Third Great King’s sinews. If you shut the gates and refuse to go out, he can transform himself. In an instant he will become a fly, enter through a crack in the gate, and drag us all outside. What shall we do then?” The old demon said, “Brothers, be vigilant. Not a single fly has entered this cave in all these years. If a fly comes in, it must be Sun the Pilgrim.” The Pilgrim laughed inwardly. “I will turn one into a fly and give them a fright. That should make them open the gates.” The Great Sage slipped aside, reached behind his head, plucked out a hair, blew a breath of immortal air upon it, and cried, “Change!” It instantly changed into a golden fly, which flew straight at the old demon and struck him squarely in the face. The old monster panicked and cried, “Brothers, this is bad! That creature has come through the gates!” All the demons, great and small, were so startled that they rushed forward with rakes and brooms, wildly swatting at the fly.

p.src: The Great Sage could contain himself no longer and burst out laughing. The trouble was that he should not have laughed, for the laugh revealed his true face. The third old demon leaped forward, seized him, and cried, “Elder Brother, he nearly deceived us!” The old demon asked, “Worthy Brother, who deceived whom?” The third monster said, “This lesser demon who just delivered the report is not Little Wind-Cleaver. He is Sun the Pilgrim himself. He must have encountered Little Wind-Cleaver and killed him somehow, then transformed himself to come and deceive us.” The Pilgrim panicked and thought, “He has recognized me.” He immediately felt himself over and said to the old monster, “How could I be Sun the Pilgrim? I am Little Wind-Cleaver. Your Majesty has mistaken me.” The old demon laughed and said, “Brother, he is Little Wind-Cleaver. He reports before me three times a day. I know him.” Then he asked, “Do you have your tally?” The Pilgrim replied, “I do.” Lifting his clothes, he took out the tally. Now even more convinced, the old monster said, “Brother, do not accuse him unjustly.” The third monster said, “Elder Brother, did you not see him? Just now, when he slipped aside and laughed, I saw his thunder-god muzzle appear. When I seized him, he changed back into this appearance.” He cried, “Minions, bring rope!” The leaders immediately fetched ropes.

p.src: The third monster threw the Pilgrim down and bound all four limbs together like a horse’s gathered hooves. When they lifted his clothes to look, there he was—the Bimawen himself. The Pilgrim, as it happened, possessed seventy-two transformations. When he changed into a bird, beast, flower, tree, vessel, insect, or the like, his entire body changed with him; but when he assumed a human form, only his head and face changed; his body could not. Sure enough, his body was covered in yellow fur, with two bare red buttocks and a tail. The old demon looked at him and said, “It is Sun the Pilgrim’s body with Little Wind-Cleaver’s face. It is indeed he.” He ordered, “Minions, first prepare wine so that we may offer your Third Great King a cup in celebration of his achievement. Now that we have captured Sun the Pilgrim, Tang Sanzang is assuredly food for our mouths.” The third monster said, “Let us not drink yet. Sun the Pilgrim is slippery and knows arts of escape. I fear he may get away. Have the minions carry out the vase and put Sun the Pilgrim inside it. Only then can we drink in peace.”

p.src: The old demon laughed loudly. “Exactly so! Exactly so!” He immediately selected thirty-six lesser demons, who went inside, opened the storeroom, and carried out the vase. How large, you may ask, was that vase? It was only two feet four inches tall. Why, then, did it take thirty-six bearers? That vase was the Treasure of the Two Primordial Breaths of Yin and Yang. Within it were the Seven Treasures, the Eight Trigrams, and the Twenty-Four Seasonal Breaths; only thirty-six bearers, corresponding to the number of the Heavenly Spirits, could move it. Before long, they carried out the precious vase, set it outside the third gate, wiped it clean, and removed its lid. They untied the Pilgrim, stripped off his clothes, and held him near the vase. With a whoosh, its immortal breath sucked him inside. They replaced the lid and pasted a seal over it. Then they went to drink, saying, “Now that the monkey has entered our precious vase, he must abandon all thought of the road to the West. If he can still worship the Buddha and obtain the scriptures, it will only be after he turns his back on the cradle, enters another womb, and takes possession of a new body.” And so, as you see, all the demons, great and small, went off smiling merrily to celebrate their victory. Of them we shall speak no more.

p.src: Now the Great Sage, once inside the bottle, found his body compressed by the treasure, so he transformed himself accordingly and crouched within. After a while he found it cool inside and suddenly laughed aloud: “These fiends have a grand reputation but no real ability. How could they tell people that anyone put into this bottle would turn to blood and pus in an hour and three quarters? If it stays as cool as this, I could live here seven or eight years without harm.” But alas! The Great Sage did not know the treasure’s secret: if a man placed inside said nothing, it would remain cool for a year; but the moment it heard a human voice, fire would come and burn him. Before the Great Sage had finished speaking, flames filled the entire bottle. Fortunately, he possessed great powers. Sitting in the middle, he formed the fire-warding spell with his fingers and was not afraid at all. After he had endured this for half an hour, forty snakes bored out from all around and began biting him. The Pilgrim swung out his hands, seized them, and with all his strength crushed each one in two, making eighty pieces in all. Soon afterward three fire dragons emerged and coiled around the Pilgrim from head to foot, proving truly hard to withstand. Growing alarmed and helpless, he said, “I can manage everything else, but these three fire dragons are troublesome. If I do not get out soon, their fiery breath will attack my heart. What shall I do?” He thought, “I shall make my body grow and burst the bottle.” The admirable Great Sage formed a spell with his fingers, recited an incantation, and cried, “Grow!” At once he grew several fathoms tall. But the bottle, clinging tightly to his body, grew along with him. When he shrank his body again, the bottle shrank with him. Startled, the Pilgrim said, “This is difficult, difficult, difficult! How is it that when I grow, it grows, and when I shrink, it shrinks? What am I to do?” Before he had finished speaking, he felt some pain in his ankle. He hastily reached down and felt it, only to find that the fire had softened it. Anxiously he said to himself, “What can I do? My ankle has been burned soft; I shall be made a cripple.” Unable to restrain himself, he shed tears. It was just as the saying goes:

p.src: He said, “Master! When I returned to the true path in years gone by, the Bodhisattva Guanyin urged me toward goodness and delivered me from Heaven’s punishment. With you I have painfully crossed mountain after mountain and destroyed many monsters; we subdued Bajie and gained Sha Monk, enduring countless hardships in the hope that together we might attain the Western Heaven and achieve the true fruit. Who could have expected that today I would meet this vicious fiend, blunder into this place, and lose my life, leaving you stranded halfway up the mountain, unable to advance? It must be because my fame was once so great that I suffer this tribulation today.”

With you I have painfully crossed mountain after mountain and destroyed many monsters; we subdued Bajie and gained Sha Monk, enduring countless hardships in the hope that together we might attain the Western Heaven and achieve the true fruit.

p.src: In the midst of his grief he suddenly remembered: “Years ago at Coiled Snake Mountain, the Bodhisattva gave me three life-saving hairs. I do not know whether they are still there; let me search for them.” He reached out and felt all over his body, and there behind his head he found three hairs, exceedingly stiff and hard. Delighted, he said, “All the hair on my body has grown soft, yet these three alone remain as hard as spears. They must surely be the ones that will save my life.” Clenching his teeth and enduring the pain, he plucked them out, breathed immortal breath upon them, and cried, “Transform!” One became a diamond-tipped drill, one a strip of bamboo, and one a cotton cord. He bent the bamboo strip into a little bow, attached the drill to it, and bored furiously at the bottom of the bottle until he made a hole through which light shone. He cried happily, “What luck! What luck! Now I can get out.” The moment he transformed himself to escape, the bottle became cool again. Why did it become cool? Because his drilling had released its yin and yang vapors, and so it cooled at once.

Because his drilling had released its yin and yang vapors, and so it cooled at once.

p.src: The admirable Great Sage put away the hairs, shrank his body, and changed into a tiny insect, nimble and light, fine as a strand of beard and as long as an eyebrow. He crawled out through the hole but did not leave; instead, he flew straight to the old fiend’s head and settled there. The old fiend was drinking wine. Suddenly setting down his cup, he asked, “Third Brother, will Sun the Pilgrim have dissolved by now?” The third fiend laughed. “How could he possibly have lasted until now?” The old fiend ordered that word be passed to carry in the bottle. The thirty-six lesser fiends below at once lifted it and found the bottle much lighter. Alarmed, the lesser fiends reported, “Your Majesty, the bottle has grown lighter.” The old fiend shouted, “Nonsense! This treasure contains the complete power of the two vapors of yin and yang. How could it have grown lighter?” One strong lesser fiend among them lifted the bottle and said, “Look—has it not grown lighter?” When the old fiend removed the lid and looked, he saw light shining through the interior and could not help crying, “The bottle is empty—empty indeed!” The Great Sage, perched on his head, could not resist adding, “My child, away means I am away!” The fiends heard him and cried, “He has escaped! He has escaped!” At once the order was passed: “Shut the gates! Shut the gates!”

p.src: Hearing these words, the Great Sage exerted himself all the more, dimmed the radiance of his cloud, drew near, and called, “Master, I have returned.” The elder took him by the arm and said, “Wukong, you have had a hard time. You went far away to scout the high mountain and did not return for so long that I was deeply worried. What good or evil truly awaits us in this mountain?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Master, on this journey just now, first, the people of the Eastern Land were blessed by destiny; second, your merit is boundless and immeasurable; and third, your disciple’s magic powers proved their worth.” He then gave a detailed account of how he had disguised himself as Little Drill-the-Wind, been trapped in the bottle, and finally escaped. “To see my honored master’s face again today is truly like returning from the dead.” The elder thanked him profusely and asked, “Did you not fight the fiends this time?” “No,” said the Pilgrim. The elder said, “Then you cannot protect me across the mountain?” The Pilgrim was a man who hated to be outdone, and he cried, “Why should I be unable to protect you across the mountain?” The elder said, “You have not settled who is stronger. With matters left so uncertain, how dare I go forward?” The Great Sage laughed. “Master, you are far too inflexible. As the saying goes, ‘A single strand makes no thread, and one hand cannot clap.’ There are three fiend kings and countless lesser fiends. How can old Sun fight them all alone?” The elder said, “The few cannot withstand the many; it is indeed difficult for you alone. Bajie and Sha Monk both have abilities of their own. Have them go too and join forces with you to clear the mountain road and protect me across.” The Pilgrim pondered and said, “Master’s words are entirely right. Let Sha Monk protect you, and have Bajie come with me.” The Idiot panicked. “Brother, you have no discernment! I am clumsy and stupid, with no great ability; I merely raise a wind when I walk. What use would I be following you?” The Pilgrim said, “Brother, though you have no great ability, at least you count as another man. As the common saying goes, ‘Even a fart adds to the wind.’ You can at least bolster my courage a little.” Bajie said, “Very well, very well. I hope you will look after me. But when danger comes suddenly, do not play tricks on me.” The elder said, “Take care, Bajie. Sha Monk and I will remain here.”

The Great Sage laughed. “Master, you are far too inflexible.
As the saying goes, ‘A single strand makes no thread, and one hand cannot clap.’
There are three fiend kings and countless lesser fiends. How can old Sun fight them all alone?”
The elder said, “The few cannot withstand the many; it is indeed difficult for you alone.
Bajie and Sha Monk both have abilities of their own. Have them go too and join forces with you to clear the mountain road and protect me across.”
The Pilgrim pondered and said, “Master’s words are entirely right.
Let Sha Monk protect you, and have Bajie come with me.”
The Idiot panicked. “Brother, you have no discernment!
I am clumsy and stupid, with no great ability; I merely raise a wind when I walk. What use would I be following you?”
The Pilgrim said, “Brother, though you have no great ability, at least you count as another man.
As the common saying goes, ‘Even a fart adds to the wind.’
You can at least bolster my courage a little.”
Bajie said, “Very well, very well. I hope you will look after me.
But when danger comes suddenly, do not play tricks on me.”
The elder said, “Take care, Bajie. Sha Monk and I will remain here.”

p.src: The fool summoned up his divine might and, together with the pilgrim, rode a raging wind and drove the clouds and mist, leaping onto the high mountain and arriving at the cave entrance. They saw at once that the cave doors were tightly shut and that no one was about. The pilgrim stepped forward, grasped his iron staff, and shouted sternly, “Open the door, demons! Come out quickly and fight old Sun!” A lesser demon within went to report this. The old demon, terrified to the very marrow, said, “For years they have said that monkey is ferocious. The tales were no lies—they are entirely true.” The second old demon beside him asked, “What do you mean, elder brother?” The old demon said, “This morning that pilgrim changed into Little Drill-the-Wind and slipped inside. We could not recognize him, but fortunately our third brother did and shut him in the bottle. He used his powers to bore through it, then spirited away his clothes and escaped. Now he is outside challenging us. Who dares fight the first bout with him?” Not a single one answered. He asked again, but still no one replied; they all pretended to be deaf and dumb. The old demon angrily said, “We have gained a certain infamous reputation on the great western road. If, after Sun the Pilgrim has treated us with such contempt today, we do not go out and face him in battle, our name will be brought low. Let me risk this old life of mine and fight him for three rounds. If I survive those three rounds, Tang Sanzang will still be food for our mouths; if I cannot, we shall shut the doors then and let him pass.” He therefore fetched his armor, arrayed himself, opened the door, and went out.

p.src: The Great Sage turned and said, “It is your Grandpa Sun, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven.” The old demon laughed. “Are you Sun the Pilgrim? You insolent wretched monkey! I have not provoked you, so why have you come here to challenge me?” The pilgrim said, “‘Only when the wind blows do waves arise; without a tide, the waters calm themselves.’ If you had not provoked me, would I have come looking for you? It is only because you and your pack of foxes and dogs banded together and plotted to eat my master that I have come here to deal with you.” The old demon said, “You have come swaggering and shouting at my gate. Can it be that you want to fight?” “Exactly,” said the pilgrim. The old demon said, “Do not be so presumptuous. If I called out my demon troops, drew them up in formation, waved flags and beat drums to battle you, it would look as though I were a tiger on its home ground taking unfair advantage of you. I shall fight you alone, one against one. No helpers are allowed.” Hearing this, the pilgrim called, “Zhu Bajie, stand aside and see what he can do to old Sun!” The fool truly did step off to one side. The old demon said, “Come here and first stand like a chopping block for me. Let me put all my strength into striking your bare head three times with my saber, and I will allow your Tang Sanzang to pass; but if you cannot endure them, quickly hand over Tang Sanzang to serve as the main dish for my meal.” The pilgrim laughed when he heard this. “Demon, if there are paper and brush in your cave, bring them out, and I will draw up an agreement with you. You may keep chopping from today until next year, and I still will not hold you to the bargain.”

p.src: The old demon raised his saber and struck again. The Great Sage thrust up his head to meet it, and with a clang he was split into two halves. The Great Sage rolled on the ground and changed into two bodies. The demon panicked at the sight and lowered the steel saber in his hand. Watching from afar, Zhu Bajie laughed and said, “That old demon is fine at chopping things in two! Does that not make four people after two strokes?” Pointing at the pilgrim, the old demon said, “I have heard you can use the art of multiplying your body. Why display that trick before me?” The Great Sage said, “What art of multiplying my body?” The old demon said, “Why did you remain unchanged when I struck you the first time, yet become two people when I struck you now?” The Great Sage laughed. “Demon, you must not be afraid. Strike me ten thousand times, and I shall give you twenty thousand men.” The old demon said, “You monkey, you can divide your body but cannot put it back together. If you have the skill to reunite yourself into one, you may strike me once with your staff.” The Great Sage said, “No going back on your word. You said you would strike me three times, but have struck me only twice. Let me strike you once; if I strike so much as half a blow more, my surname is not Sun.” “Quite so, quite so,” said the old demon.

p.src: Now Bajie, watching below as the two fought at their fiercest, could restrain himself no longer. He drew his rake, mounted the wind, leaped up, and brought it down straight at the demon’s face. The demon panicked. He did not know that Bajie was merely rash and blustering by nature, charging heedlessly to frighten people. He saw only the long snout, great ears, strong arms, and ferocious rake; so he abandoned the fight, dropped his saber, turned, and fled. The Great Sage shouted, “After him! After him!” Emboldened by his success, the fool raised his nine-pronged rake and hurried after the monster. When the old demon saw him drawing close, he stopped before the slope, faced into the wind, shook himself, and revealed his original form. Opening his enormous mouth, he moved to swallow Bajie. Terrified, Bajie hastily wheeled about and plunged into the grass, heedless of thorn and bramble and caring nothing that they scratched his head painfully. Trembling in the grass, he listened to the clacking sounds outside. The pilgrim arrived in pursuit soon afterward. The monster opened his mouth to swallow him too, but fell into the pilgrim’s trap: the pilgrim put away his iron staff and went straight to meet him, and the old demon swallowed him in one gulp. The fool, terrified in the grass, muttered and grumbled, “That Protector of the Horses never knows when to advance or retreat. When the monster came to eat you, why did you not run away, but instead went forward to meet him? Once swallowed into his belly like that, today you may still be a monk, but tomorrow you will be a great heap of dung.” The demon departed victorious. Only then did the fool crawl out of the grass and slink back along the way he had come.

p.src: Meanwhile, Tripitaka was waiting with Sha Monk below the hillside when Bajie came running back, panting heavily. Greatly alarmed, Tripitaka said, “Bajie, how did you come to be in such a sorry state? And why is Wukong nowhere to be seen?” The fool sobbed, “Elder Brother was swallowed whole by the monster.” At these words Tripitaka collapsed to the ground. After a long while he stamped his feet and beat his breast, crying, “Disciple! I thought you were so skilled at subduing monsters that you would lead me to the Western Heaven to behold the Buddha. How could I have known that today you would die at this fiend’s hands? What misery! What misery! All the labors of my disciples and companions have now turned to dust.” The master was overwhelmed with grief. But look at that fool: instead of consoling his master, he called out, “Sha Monk, bring the luggage over and let the two of us divide it.” Sha Monk asked, “Second Brother, why should we divide it?” Bajie said, “Once we have divided it, we can each go our separate way. You can return to the River of Flowing Sands and go back to eating people; I shall go to Gao Village and visit my wife. We can sell the white horse and buy Master a coffin to see him properly buried.” When the elder heard this, he trembled with rage, cried out to Heaven, and burst into loud weeping. But let us speak no more of that.

p.src: Now the old demon, believing his scheme had succeeded after swallowing the Pilgrim, went straight back to his cave, where the other demons welcomed him and asked how the battle had gone. The old demon said, “I caught one of them.” Delighted, the second demon asked, “Who did you catch, Elder Brother?” The old demon replied, “Sun the Pilgrim.” The second demon asked, “Where are you holding him?” The old demon said, “I swallowed him whole into my belly.” The third demon exclaimed in alarm, “Elder Brother! Did I not warn you that Sun the Pilgrim is unfit to eat?” From inside his belly the Great Sage said, “I am wonderfully fit to eat. I fill the stomach and keep hunger away.” The lesser demons cried in panic, “Your Majesty, this is terrible! Sun the Pilgrim is talking inside your belly!” The old demon said, “Why fear his talking? If I have the skill to eat him, do you think I lack the skill to deal with him? Quickly prepare some hot salt water. I shall pour it into my stomach and vomit him out, then slowly fry him to go with our wine.” The lesser demons duly mixed half a basin of salt water. The old monster drained it at one draught, opened his mouth wide, and heaved with all his might; but the Great Sage had rooted himself inside the belly and did not budge. The demon then strained his throat and tried again to vomit him out, retching until his head spun, his eyes blurred, and even his gallbladder nearly burst; yet the Pilgrim remained more motionless than ever. Panting for breath, the old demon called, “Sun the Pilgrim, will you not come out?” The Pilgrim answered, “It is far too early. I am quite content not to come out!” The old demon asked, “Why will you not come out?” The Pilgrim said, “You monster have no understanding of circumstances. Ever since I became a monk, I have lived most austerely. Now autumn is growing cold, yet I still wear only an unlined robe. It is warm here in your belly, and no wind gets through. I shall spend the winter here before I come out.”

p.src: When the demons heard this, they all said, “Your Majesty, Sun the Pilgrim intends to spend the winter in your belly!” The old demon said, “If he means to winter there, I shall enter meditation and use the art of sustaining myself without food. I shall eat nothing all winter and starve that Stable-Boy to death.” The Great Sage said, “My son, you know nothing. While escorting the Tang Monk to fetch the scriptures, old Sun passed through Guangli and brought along a folding pot. I shall set it up in here and cook your innards to eat. I shall leisurely enjoy your liver, intestines, stomach, and lungs. They will provide ample provisions to last me until the Qingming Festival.” The second demon exclaimed in alarm, “Brother, that monkey is perfectly capable of doing it!” The third demon said, “Brother, never mind if he eats the innards—but where will he set up his pot?” The Pilgrim replied, “The three-pronged breastbone is an excellent place to set a pot.” The third demon said, “This is terrible! If he sets up the pot and lights a fire, the smoke will rise into your nostrils and make you sneeze, will it not?” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “That is no problem. Old Sun will thrust his golden-hooped staff up through the crown of his head and make a hole: it will serve both as a skylight and as a chimney.”

p.src: Though the old demon claimed not to be afraid, his heart quailed when he heard this. Steeling himself, he called, “Brothers, do not be afraid. Bring me my medicated wine. I shall drink a few cups and poison the monkey to death.” The Pilgrim laughed inwardly and thought, “Five hundred years ago, when old Sun made havoc in Heaven, I ate Lord Lao’s elixir, drank the Jade Emperor’s wine, and consumed the Queen Mother’s peaches, as well as phoenix marrow and dragon liver. What delicacy have I not tasted? What sort of medicated wine could possibly poison me?” The lesser demons duly warmed two pots of medicated wine, filled a cup to the brim, and handed it to the old demon. The old demon took it in his hand. Smelling the wine’s fragrance from inside the belly, the Great Sage said, “Do not let him drink it.” The splendid Great Sage twisted his head and changed his mouth into the shape of a trumpet, holding it open just below the demon’s throat. The monster gulped down the wine, and the Pilgrim caught and drank it with a gulp of his own. The second cup went down, and the Pilgrim again caught and drank it with a gulp. The demon drank seven or eight cups in succession, and the Pilgrim caught and drank every one. The old demon put down the cup and said, “I shall drink no more. Usually, after two cups of this wine, my belly burns like fire; yet I have just drunk seven or eight, and my face is not even flushed!”

p.src: As it happened, the Great Sage could not hold much liquor. After catching and drinking the demon’s seven or eight cups, he began raising a drunken riot inside the belly: striking martial poses, sprawling flat on his back, kicking his feet through the air, seizing a lobe of the liver and using it as a swing, standing on his head, turning somersaults, and wildly cavorting about. The monster could not endure the agony and collapsed to the ground.
